title: Pier Seventeen
tagline: Fog on the water, a clerk at the foot of the stairs, and a carbon copy of everything.
setting: The Ashgrove Shipping harbor office at Pier Seventeen on the Calder City waterfront
intro_briefing: April 1949. The fog has sat on the Calder City waterfront for three days, thick enough to lose a freighter in. At six this morning the night watchman at Pier Seventeen found Harold Pike, 58, chief clerk of Ashgrove Shipping for thirty-one years, at the foot of the iron stairs in the ledger archive.

It was phoned in as a fall. The police surgeon does not like it: one deep blow to the left temple that the steps did not give him. He puts death between a quarter to eleven and half past eleven last night.

Four people are waiting for you in the harbor office. Clara Ashgrove, who has run Ashgrove Shipping since her father's death. Leonard Vance of Vance and Pryor, the firm's attorney, whom Clara telephoned before she telephoned anyone else. Inspector Ruth Calloway of Harbor Customs, here since dawn to seal the bonded warehouse as regulation requires. And Tommy Reyes, the watchman, who smells of peppermints at seven in the morning.

Patrolman Duffy took first statements at dawn and has been checking what he could; anything he brought back is on the front office counter. Search the office, the archive, the warehouse, the dock and the gatehouse. Question all four, show them what you find, and pin every story to the clock. When you know who sent Harold Pike down those stairs, and can prove it, make your accusation.

victim.name: Harold Pike
victim.description: Chief clerk of Ashgrove Shipping for thirty-one years, a widower who lived for his ledgers and was known on the waterfront for keeping a carbon copy of nearly everything he wrote.
victim.cause_of_death: A single heavy blow to the left temple and a broken neck at the foot of the archive stairs, first reported as a fall. The police surgeon puts death between 22:45 and 23:30.
victim.found_at: at 06:00 by the night watchman, at the foot of the iron stairs

solution.motive: Harold Pike had matched Inspector Ruth Calloway's customs clearances to falsified manifests on six Ashgrove sailings, proof that she had been taking bribes to pass smuggled cargo, and he meant to hand them to the Harbor Commission at nine in the morning.
solution.method: After Pike telephoned her at 22:45, Calloway signed out of the Customs House at 22:50, let herself into the pier through the warehouse wicket with her inspector's key, struck Pike on the temple with the iron ledger press in the archive, pushed him down the stairs to stage a fall, and left with the stamped manifests, missing the carbon copy on his tally board.
solution.reveal: Harold Pike spent his last evening doing what he had done for thirty-one years: checking the paper against the cargo. At 20:15 he counted the Mary Delacroix's crates against his carbon copy of the manifest, found twelve chalk-marked crates of rye cleared as machine parts, and saw in the customs block the same signature that had cleared five other Ashgrove sailings since November: R. Calloway, No. 114. Leonard Vance came at ten to buy back Pike's dossier on the trust money he had taken; he lost a cufflink at the steel cabinet, left at half past ten and sailed on the 22:40 ferry to Eastbank, with no way back before 23:50. At 22:45 Pike, a decent man to the end, telephoned Ruth Calloway to warn her the commission would have her clearances at nine. She signed out of the Customs House at 22:50, walked ten minutes through the fog, let herself in at the warehouse wicket with her inspector's key and found him in the archive. When he would not give up the folder she hit him with the iron ledger press, sent him down the stairs to make it a fall, set the press back on its shelf with customs violet still on the grip, and walked out under the pier lamp in her rain cape at ten past eleven, where a watchman who should have been on his rounds saw her from the gatehouse window. She burned the stamped manifests; she never knew about the carbon on his tally board. Clara Ashgrove buried a warning to save her company, but she was on the Mariners' Club telephone at eleven. Tommy Reyes drank through his shift and robbed a body that was already cold. The carbon gives the motive, the press the means, the night book breaks her alibi and Tommy's sighting puts her on the pier: only Ruth Calloway had both the reason in the manifests and the hour after 22:50.

timeline.what: Harold Pike tells Clara Ashgrove he will take the customs clearances on six Ashgrove sailings to the Harbor Commission at nine tomorrow morning. She forbids it and they quarrel.
The freighter Mary Delacroix finishes unloading forty crates of machine parts into the warehouse. Inspector Calloway signs the customs clearance on the pier while Pike watches.
Inspector Calloway signs in for evening duty at the Customs House.
Clara Ashgrove arrives at the Mariners' Club dinner for the harbor commissioners.
Tommy Reyes comes on shift at the gatehouse and keys the first watch station.
Pike counts the Delacroix crates against his carbon copy of the manifest, finds twelve chalk-marked crates and pries one open: Canadian rye.
Tommy keys the nine o'clock station, then settles into the gatehouse with a bottle of gin and walks no more rounds.
Leonard Vance meets Pike in the archive to buy back the dossier on the Ashgrove trust. Pike refuses and catches his sleeve when Vance reaches for the folder at the steel cabinet.
Vance leaves empty-handed. Pike goes back to his desk with a folder of cargo manifests and the telephone directory.
From the gatehouse window Tommy sees a gentleman in a gray homburg hurry out through the main gate toward the ferry slip.
Vance sails on the 22:40 Eastbank ferry from the end of the pier on his firm's account ticket.
Pike telephones Inspector Calloway at the Customs House and tells her he is taking her clearances to the Harbor Commission at nine.
Ruth Calloway signs out of the Customs House night book.
Clara Ashgrove telephones the gatehouse from the Mariners' Club to ask whether Pike is still at the office. Tommy answers and writes the call on the pad.

Let in by her own key at the warehouse wicket, Ruth Calloway confronts Pike in the archive, strikes him with the iron ledger press, pushes him down the stairs and takes the folder of stamped manifests.
From the gatehouse window Tommy sees a figure in a long customs rain cape cross under the pier lamp toward the warehouse wicket.
Tommy Reyes finds Harold Pike dead at the foot of the archive stairs.
Tommy takes Pike's wallet from his jacket before going to telephone the police.
Clara Ashgrove and Inspector Calloway arrive at the pier office; Leonard Vance follows at ten past seven. Patrolman Duffy takes their statements.

offstage_locations.name: The Mariners' Club on Harbor Hill

rooms.name: Front Office
rooms.description: Ashgrove Shipping's front office: oak counters, brass lamps gone green at the joints, and a wall of tide tables and sailing schedules. The clerks' desks are empty this morning. A short passage at the back leads to the ledger archive.

hotspots.label: Window
hotspots.description: The window looks down the whole length of Pier Seventeen, or would, if the fog allowed it. You can just make out the single lamp halfway down the pier and the dark box of the gatehouse beyond it. Somebody wrote 'P.17' in the condensation years ago, and it comes back every damp night.

hotspots.label: Filing cabinet
hotspots.description: A green steel cabinet with Clara Ashgrove's card on the top drawer. The bottom drawer is locked, but the key is on the ring she left on her blotter. Under a stack of insurance renewals lies a typed memo with a line of green ink across the top.

hotspots.label: Wall telephone
hotspots.description: The office telephone, with a pencil hanging on a string and a pad beside it. The top sheet has been torn away, but Pike always pressed hard. Tilted to the light, the next sheet carries the ghost of his last note: '10.45 - Cust. Ho. - told her.'

hotspots.label: Typewriter
hotspots.description: Pike's Underwood, dusted daily. A sheet is still rolled in: 'To the Secretary, Calder Harbor Commission. Sir, I beg to lay before the Commission evidence that the customs clearances on six Ashgrove sailings since November' and there it stops, mid-line. Beside it sits an empty wire tray labeled FOR THE COMMISSION.

hotspots.label: Sign-out ledger
hotspots.description: Patrolman Duffy's legwork, left on the front counter with a note in his round hand: 'Borrowed from the Customs House night porter, 7.20 a.m. Thought you would want it. D.' A heavy book, open at last night's page.

rooms.name: Ledger Archive
rooms.description: A long, low room of bound ledgers that smells of glue, paper and old harbor damp. At the far end, steep iron stairs drop to the lower stacks. This is where Harold Pike was found.

hotspots.label: Ledger shelf
hotspots.description: Rows of cargo ledgers going back to 1907, every spine lettered in Pike's hand. A cast-iron press sits at the end of the third shelf, on the wrong side of the row, as if someone put it back in a hurry. You lift it. It is heavy enough to hurt your wrist.

hotspots.label: Steel cabinet
hotspots.description: A tall steel cabinet with its top drawer pulled half open. Pike's index card on the front lists a folder, 'Delacroix et al., for the Commission', that is not in any drawer. Another folder is still here: thick, manila, and labeled with someone else's initials.

hotspots.label: Lamp
hotspots.description: A green-shaded lamp on a long flex over the binding table, still burning when the watchman came in at six. Its light makes the dust hang like smoke. Every page Pike ever checked, he checked under this lamp.

hotspots.label: Binding table
hotspots.description: A scarred oak table with glue pots and a bone folder. In the dust there is a clean square where something heavy usually sits. Under the table, against the leg nearest the stairs, something small and gold catches the lamplight.

hotspots.label: Stairs
hotspots.description: Steep iron stairs drop to the lower stacks, and a chalk outline lies at the bottom. The police surgeon's note is pinned to the rail: one deep wound to the left temple, a broken neck, and not one of the iron edges shows blood or hair. A man who falls breaks his neck. He does not usually dent his own temple on the way down.

rooms.name: Pier and Loading Dock
rooms.description: Pier Seventeen in the fog: wet planks, black water, the Mary Delacroix riding high at her lines, and at the far end the ferry slip for the Eastbank crossing.

hotspots.label: Ferry clock
hotspots.description: A big clock face over the ferry gate, with the Eastbank timetable painted beneath it: departures 21:40, 22:40, 23:50, then nothing until 06:10. The crossing takes twenty minutes each way, and each boat lies over at Eastbank before it comes back for the next sailing. By road, round the head of the harbor, it is the best part of an hour.

hotspots.label: Pier lamp
hotspots.description: The only lamp on Pier Seventeen, halfway between the office door and the warehouse wicket. Anyone crossing between them walks through its circle of light, and the gatehouse window looks straight at it.

hotspots.label: Slip ledger
hotspots.description: The ferry slip-man's booth is shut until the first crossing, but his tally book hangs on a nail inside the hatch, every departure written up in pencil with the fares and the account tickets.

hotspots.label: Mooring rope
hotspots.description: The Mary Delacroix's lines creak against the bollards. Her crew are ashore, and her mate has told Patrolman Duffy twice that nobody aboard saw a thing. The water under the pier is black and very deep.

rooms.name: Cargo Warehouse
rooms.description: The bonded cargo warehouse, cold as a church. The Mary Delacroix's crates stand in rows under the high windows, cleared by customs yesterday afternoon and waiting for their carters.

hotspots.label: Rope and hooks
hotspots.description: Coils of manila rope and a rack of longshoremen's iron cargo hooks: twelve pegs and twelve hooks, each one dull with oil and none of them marked. Whatever hit Harold Pike, it was not one of these.

hotspots.label: Freight door
hotspots.description: The big sliding freight door is chained from inside. Beside it is a narrow side wicket that opens straight onto Front Street, outside the pier gate, so nobody using it passes the gatehouse. Its brass customs lock is regulation for bonded premises: it opens only to the chief clerk's key and to the keys every customs inspector carries. There is fresh street mud on the sill, inside.

hotspots.label: Crates
hotspots.description: Forty crates stencilled MACHINE PARTS - ROTTERDAM, stacked where the Delacroix's crew left them. Twelve carry a small chalk X on the end. One of the twelve has had its lid pried up and nailed down again. Inside, packed in straw: bottles of Canadian rye.

hotspots.label: Tally desk
hotspots.description: Pike's high, sloped tally desk, where he checked cargo against paper. A clipboard hangs from a nail on its side with a thin carbon flimsy under the clip and a pencil tied on with string.

rooms.name: Watchman's Gatehouse
rooms.description: A wooden booth at the landward end of the pier with a stove, a stool, a cot and one window that looks over everything. Tommy Reyes has spent eleven years of nights in here.

hotspots.label: Window
hotspots.description: From the watchman's stool the window takes in the whole pier: the main gate, the office door, the lamp halfway down, the warehouse wicket at the far end. In fog you would see a shape and a color under that lamp, never a face. The stool is worn smooth.

hotspots.label: Coat
hotspots.description: Tommy's heavy pea coat on its hook, smelling of wet wool and peppermint. Something square and stiff has been stuffed deep into the inside pocket.

hotspots.label: Watchman's clock
hotspots.description: A leather-cased watchman's clock on its strap. Every station on the pier has a key on a chain; turn it in the clock and it punches the time onto a paper dial inside. Company rule says the dial is changed every morning at six. Nobody has changed this one yet.

hotspots.label: Phone
hotspots.description: A wall telephone with a pad on a string beside it and a card in Pike's careful lettering: ALL CALLS TO THE GATE TO BE WRITTEN DOWN. H.P.

hotspots.label: Bottle
hotspots.description: A bottle of Old Harbor gin with two fingers left and a tin cup with a ring in the bottom. Behind them sits a paper bag of peppermints, half gone.

evidence.name: Carbon copy manifest
evidence.description: A carbon flimsy of the Mary Delacroix's cargo manifest: forty crates, machine parts, Rotterdam. The customs clearance block has come through in carbon: 'Examined and found correct. R. Calloway, Inspector No. 114.' Beneath it, in Pike's pencil: 'Counted 20.15. Twelve crates chalked X. Opened one: rye. Same inspector on all six sailings. Commission, 9 a.m.' The stamped originals are not in the office or the archive.

evidence.name: Iron ledger press
evidence.description: A cast-iron hand press the size of a brick, with a ring handle, used to weigh down ledgers while the bindings set. Its clean square in the dust of the binding table is empty; it was put back on the wrong shelf. Dried blood and two gray hairs are packed into the crease of the ring, and on the grip there is a smear of bright violet ink with the fine crosshatch of a woven glove pressed into it: the aniline violet of customs clearance stamps. Ashgrove's own office stamps are black.

evidence.name: Customs House night book
evidence.description: The Calder City Customs House sign-out book for last night, borrowed from the night porter by Patrolman Duffy. Six inspectors signed in for the evening. Haskins out 00:40, Morrow out 01:15, and in a neat upright hand: 'R. Calloway, No. 114. In 18.00. Out 22.50.' Calloway is the only woman on the evening roster. The Customs House stands at the head of the waterfront, ten minutes' walk from Pier Seventeen.

evidence.name: Tommy's sighting
evidence.description: Tommy Reyes's account, once he admitted he never left the gatehouse: at about ten past eleven, just after six bells on the Delacroix, a figure in a long navy customs rain cape, hood up, walked fast under the pier lamp from the office door toward the warehouse side wicket. He took it for an inspector checking seals and went back to his bottle.

evidence.name: Pike's trust dossier
evidence.description: A manila folder labeled in Pike's hand 'L.V. - Ashgrove Family Trust'. Inside: trust ledger extracts, photostats of checks signed by Leonard Vance as trustee, and photostats of a green ledger kept at the Blue Lantern club, showing the same sums paid in by 'L.V.' and paid out again as band fees. A total is underlined twice: $23,400. Clipped to the front: 'Put right by May 1st, or it goes to the Bar Association.'

evidence.name: Gold cufflink
evidence.description: A gold oval cufflink engraved 'L.V.', its swivel bar bent as if it had been torn from a cuff, lying under the binding table a few feet from the head of the stairs. The charwoman sweeps the archive every evening at six.

evidence.name: Pike's wallet
evidence.description: A worn pigskin wallet with Harold Pike's identity card and eleven dollars folded inside, stuffed deep into the inside pocket of the watchman's coat. The leather is still damp from the archive floor.

evidence.name: Pike's March memo
evidence.description: A typed memo from H. Pike to Miss C. Ashgrove, dated 14 March 1949: 'Customs clearances on six of our sailings do not agree with the warehouse tallies. All six bear the same inspector's signature. I must ask your leave to lay this before the Harbor Commission.' Across the top, in green ink: 'File. Not now. C.A.'

evidence.name: Watchman's clock dial
evidence.description: The paper dial from Tommy's watchman's clock. Stations punched at 20:00, 20:30 and 21:00. Then nothing at all until 05:30: eight and a half hours of blank ring on a night a man died on his pier.

evidence.name: Ferry slip tally book
evidence.description: The slip-man's pencilled tally for the Eastbank ferry that sails from the end of Pier Seventeen. '22.40 dep. Eastbank, 23 fares. Acct. ticket No. 417, Vance and Pryor, 1 gent, punched.' The 22:40 boat does not tie up at Pier Seventeen again until 23:50.

evidence.name: Gatehouse telephone pad
evidence.description: The pad by the gatehouse telephone, in Tommy's shaky capitals: '11 PM. MISS ASHGROVE FROM MARINERS CLUB. CLUB OPERATOR PUT HER THROUGH. IS MR PIKE STILL IN. TOLD HER LIGHTS ON.' Why the head of the firm was checking on her clerk at eleven at night, the pad does not say.

suspects.name: Leonard Vance
suspects.role: Attorney-at-law of Vance and Pryor, counsel to Ashgrove Shipping and trustee of the Ashgrove Family Trust
suspects.personality: Smooth, precise and unfailingly polite, a man who has spent thirty years making other people's trouble sound like paperwork. He never raises his voice; when cornered he grows more courteous, not less. Since February, when his statement put a nightclub manager in the dock, his name has been in the papers more often than he likes. Vain about his reputation, frightened for it this morning, and far too proud to show either.
suspects.speech_style: Measured, lawyerly sentences with qualifications stacked like files: 'strictly speaking', 'as a matter of form', 'I would put it rather differently'. Reaches for a Latin tag when he wants distance (res ipsa loquitur, caveat emptor, de minimis). Calls the detective 'Detective' with a faint smile and answers a question with a question whenever he can.
suspects.alibi: I spent the evening at home in Eastbank with a brief and a glass of port. Strictly speaking, I had not set foot on Pier Seventeen in a month until Miss Ashgrove telephoned me this morning.
public_facts: Leonard Vance of Vance and Pryor has been Ashgrove Shipping's attorney for twenty years and administers the Ashgrove Family Trust.
Clara Ashgrove telephoned him at dawn; he arrived at the pier at ten past seven, freshly shaved, in a gray homburg.
private_knowledge: Harold Pike had put together a folder proving that you have been drawing money from the Ashgrove trust since 1945 and passing it through the Blue Lantern's books as band fees. After Victor Kale was shot in February, the club's green ledger went to his estate's accountants, and somehow Pike got photostats of it. He gave you until the first of May to repay it before he went to the Bar Association.

You went to the archive at ten last night to buy the folder back. Pike would not sell at any price and told you the Harbor Commission would hear 'the customs business' at nine in the morning, and you could wait your turn.
When you reached for the folder at the steel cabinet, Pike caught your sleeve. Your cufflink must have come loose then.
When you left at half past ten, Pike was alive and back at his desk with a folder of cargo manifests and the telephone directory open at the Customs House page.
You sailed on the 22:40 Eastbank ferry on the firm's account ticket and were home before half past eleven. Your housekeeper was asleep.

lies.claim: At home in Eastbank all evening with a brief and a glass of port, nowhere near Pier Seventeen.
lies.truth: You were with Harold Pike in the archive from ten until half past ten, then caught the 22:40 Eastbank ferry from the end of the pier.

lies.claim: The trust is in perfect order and audited every year. Mr. Pike had no business with it.
lies.truth: You have quietly borrowed more than twenty thousand dollars from it, and Pike had the proof in a folder with your initials on it.

secrets: Your left eye has been failing for a year. You read contracts behind a locked door with a jeweler's glass and have told no one, not even your partner Pryor.
never_reveal: The full sum you took from the Ashgrove trust and where every dollar of it went.
That you carried an envelope of cash to the archive last night, hoping Pike would take it.

revealable_clues.text: Remarks that Harold Pike was the most meticulous clerk on the waterfront and kept a carbon copy of every paper he ever touched: belt and braces, strictly speaking.

Admits he met Pike in the archive at ten last night, that Pike caught his sleeve at the steel cabinet, and that he left at half past ten for the 22:40 Eastbank ferry. Pike was alive and back at his desk with a folder of cargo manifests and the telephone directory open at the Customs House page.
Admits the Vance and Pryor account ticket in the slip-man's book is his: he sailed to Eastbank at 22:40 and could not have come back before the 23:50 crossing. Pike was alive when he left the pier.

Admits Pike had given him until the first of May to repay the trust or face the Bar Association. He went to settle it privately; Pike would not sell the folder and said the Harbor Commission would hear 'the customs business' first, at nine, and Vance could wait his turn.

Says that when Pike telephoned him last week, the old clerk mentioned he had found 'something rotten in the customs paper' on Ashgrove sailings and meant to see it through, whatever it cost the firm. Pike would not say whose signature was on it.

deflections: *polishes his spectacles with great care*  Strictly speaking, Detective, that question has no proper answer. Try me with a better one.
*smiles thinly*  Res ipsa loquitur. Or rather, it does not. Ask me something else.
I would be delighted to help you, Detective, the moment you ask me something I am obliged to answer.
*consults his pocket watch*  Caveat emptor. I give nothing away before nine, not even an opinion.

alibi_verification.note: Vance lied about never being at the pier: the cufflink puts him in the archive and his dossier gives him a motive. But the ferry slip tally book shows his account ticket punched on the 22:40 crossing to Eastbank, with no boat back before 23:50 and an hour by road, and Tommy saw him go out the gate toward the slip at about 22:35. Pike was still alive at 22:45, when he telephoned the Customs House, so Vance's night on the pier ended before the death window opened.

suspects.name: Clara Ashgrove
suspects.personality: Sharp, proud and controlled. Last October she buried her father and saw her husband taken away in handcuffs in the same week, then took her father's chair over the heads of a board that wanted the man from Boston, and she has spent every day since proving them wrong. She treats the Ashgrove name as something entrusted to her, and will lie to protect it before she would lie to protect herself. Grief and anger both stay behind her teeth.
suspects.speech_style: Clipped, exact sentences with no wasted words and no softening. Says 'my father's firm' and 'Ashgrove' as though they were one word, and still calls him 'Father', never 'Dad'. Corrects imprecision ('Not quite, Detective'). Goes quieter, not louder, when she is angry, and never says please.
suspects.alibi: I was at the Mariners' Club dinner for the harbor commissioners from half past seven until half past eleven, then took a taxi home to the Heights.
public_facts: Clara Ashgrove has run Ashgrove Shipping since her father's death last October.
She attended the Mariners' Club dinner for the harbor commissioners last night.
Ashgrove Shipping is in the middle of negotiating new coastal mail contracts with the Harbor Commission.
private_knowledge: Harold Pike came to you at four yesterday afternoon and said he would go to the Harbor Commission at nine this morning about the customs clearances, with or without your leave. You forbade it.

At eleven you telephoned the gatehouse from the Mariners' Club to ask whether Pike was still at the office. You meant to drive down after the dinner and talk him round, but the watchman slurred that the light was on and you lost your nerve.
You left the club at half past eleven in a taxi with Commissioner Brennan.
Pike never told you which customs inspector signed the clearances. He said he wanted to be certain first.

Your father meant to make you trustee of the family trust in Leonard Vance's place, but he died before he signed the papers. Twice since Christmas you have asked Vance for a full accounting of the trust, and twice he has put you off with a smile.

lies.claim: I knew nothing about any problem with our manifests until this morning.
lies.truth: Pike warned you in a memo in March that customs clearances on six sailings did not match the warehouse counts. You wrote 'File. Not now.' across it and locked it away to protect the coastal contracts.

lies.claim: Harold and I had not spoken in days. We were on perfectly good terms.
lies.truth: You quarrelled with him at four yesterday when he said he would go to the commission, and you telephoned the gatehouse at eleven to see if he was still at the office.

secrets: In January you quietly mortgaged Ashgrove House, your father's house on the cliffs, to meet the firm's payroll. The board does not know.
never_reveal: That Ashgrove Shipping will be bankrupt by the summer without the coastal mail contracts.

revealable_clues.text: States that she was at the Mariners' Club dinner for the harbor commissioners until half past eleven and shared a taxi home with Commissioner Brennan.
Admits she and Pike had words at four o'clock yesterday about papers he wanted to take outside the firm. She will not say which papers.

Admits she telephoned the gatehouse from the Mariners' Club at eleven to ask whether Pike was still at the office, meaning to talk him out of going to the commission. The watchman answered, slurring, and said the light was on.

Admits Pike's March memo warned her that customs clearances on six Ashgrove sailings did not agree with the warehouse counts and all carried the same inspector's signature, and that she buried it to protect the coastal contracts. Pike never told her the inspector's name.

deflections: *straightens a pen on the desk until it lies exactly parallel*  I have answered that, Detective. I do not repeat myself.
My father's firm has outlasted better questions than that one. Next.
*looks at the fog pressing on the window*  Not now.

alibi_verification.note: Her motive is real: she buried Pike's memo to protect the company. But the gatehouse telephone pad and Tommy both put her on the Mariners' Club line at 23:00, across town, in the middle of the death window, and she left the club at 23:30 with Commissioner Brennan.

suspects.name: Ruth Calloway
suspects.personality: Cool, precise and admired: the one inspector the waterfront swears cannot be bought, a reputation she has built brick by brick. Patient and observant, never flustered in public. Underneath runs a cold arithmetic; she weighs every answer for what it will cost before she gives it, and she has nothing but contempt for sloppiness, her own included.
suspects.speech_style: Short, exact declaratives. Gives times to the minute and cites regulations by number ('Section 14, bonded premises'). Says 'Correct', 'For the record' and 'Noted'. Never fills a silence. When a question lands too close she smooths her gloves and answers a slightly different question.
suspects.alibi: I was at the Customs House filing the week's clearance reports until well past midnight. Then I went home to bed.
public_facts: Inspector Ruth Calloway has cleared cargo on the Ashgrove piers for six years and is the most respected inspector in the Calder City Customs Service.
She cleared the freighter Mary Delacroix's forty crates of machine parts on the pier at half past five yesterday.
She came to Pier Seventeen at a quarter to seven this morning to seal the bonded warehouse, as regulation requires after a death on bonded premises.
private_knowledge: Every customs inspector carries a key to the side wickets of the bonded warehouses on the waterfront, Pier Seventeen's included.
You wore your navy customs rain cape all night because of the fog.
Since November you have been paid to clear chalk-marked crates of rye whiskey and cigarettes as machine parts on Ashgrove sailings.
Harold Pike watched you sign the Delacroix clearance yesterday afternoon and did not say a word.

lies.claim: At the Customs House filing clearance reports until well past midnight, then home to bed.
lies.truth: You signed out at ten to eleven, walked down to Pier Seventeen in the fog and let yourself in at the warehouse side wicket with your inspector's key.

lies.claim: Every Ashgrove cargo I cleared was examined and found correct.
lies.truth: Since November you have taken money to pass chalk-marked crates of rye whiskey and cigarettes as machine parts on six Ashgrove sailings.

lies.claim: I knew him to nod to on the pier. We had no business beyond the paperwork.
lies.truth: He rang you at a quarter to eleven last night to warn you that your clearances were going to the Harbor Commission at nine.

secrets: In 1941 you were engaged to a merchant seaman who went down on an Arctic convoy, and you still wear his ring on a chain under your collar.
never_reveal: That when Pike would not give you the folder you swung the iron press from the shelf into the side of his head, then tipped him down the iron stairs so it would read as a fall, and set the press back where it lived.
That you burned the stamped manifests in your kitchen stove before one in the morning.
The names of the men who pay you.

revealable_clues.text: Remarks, as a point of regulation, that inspectors are issued a long navy rain cape with a hood and a brass clasp, and that she wore hers all last night in the fog.
Concedes that every customs inspector carries a key to the side wickets of the bonded warehouses, Pier Seventeen's included.

Faced with the carbon, admits Pike telephoned her at the Customs House at a quarter to eleven last night to say he was taking her clearances to the Harbor Commission at nine. Insists she put the receiver down and stayed at her desk.
Faced with the night book, admits she signed out at ten to eleven, then claims she walked home along Front Street in the fog to clear her head and spoke to no one.
Concedes the violet smear is customs clearance ink, the same that stains her gloves every working day, but says any clerk who handles cleared manifests could carry it.

deflections: *smooths her gloves, finger by finger*  For the record, Detective, I have answered that. Noted, and declined.
Section 14, bonded premises: I am not required to speculate. I would hope you are not either.
*watches the fog move on the water*  You are wasting the tide. Ask me something with a time in it.

alibi_verification.note: She claims she was at the Customs House until past midnight. The night book shows her signed out at 22:50, five minutes after Pike telephoned her and ten minutes' walk from Pier Seventeen, and Tommy saw a figure in a customs rain cape cross under the pier lamp toward the warehouse wicket at about 23:10, inside the death window.

suspects.name: Tommy Reyes
suspects.personality: A big, soft, tired man who has guarded the same gate for eleven years and the same bottle for longer. Kind, ashamed and eager to please, frightened of losing the job and the cot that comes with it. He lies the way a child does: badly, then far too much.
suspects.speech_style: Rambling waterfront talk in long run-on sentences that circle back on themselves. Calls the detective 'chief' or 'Detective, sir'. Tells time by ship's bells ('six bells on the Delacroix'). Says 'I tell you true' right before a lie. Sucks peppermints between sentences and loses his thread.
suspects.alibi: I walked my rounds all night, chief, every station, regular as the tide: warehouse, dock, office and back to the gate.
public_facts: Tommy Reyes has been the night watchman at Pier Seventeen for eleven years and sleeps on a cot in the gatehouse.
He found Harold Pike at the foot of the archive stairs at six this morning and telephoned the police.
The whole waterfront knows Tommy keeps a bottle somewhere about him.
private_knowledge: You stopped walking your rounds at nine and spent the whole night in the gatehouse with a bottle of gin.
From the gatehouse window you can see the whole pier: the main gate, the office door, the single lamp halfway down and the warehouse wicket.
When you found Mr. Pike at six he was cold and stiff. You took his wallet before you telephoned: eleven dollars, and you owe the rent.
Mr. Pike was good to you. He knew about the drinking and never reported it.

lies.claim: Walked every station all night, regular as the tide.
lies.truth: You keyed the last station at nine and never left the gatehouse until half past five. You were drinking.

lies.claim: Never saw it. Somebody must have robbed the poor man.
lies.truth: You took it from his jacket when you found him at six and stuffed it into your coat.

secrets: You have a daughter in Portland who has not written in nine years. You send her a birthday card every March anyway.
never_reveal: That the Merchant Marine put you ashore in 1931 for being drunk on watch.

revealable_clues.text: Explains, proud of knowing his pier, that the warehouse side wicket opens straight onto Front Street outside the main gate, so anybody with Mr. Pike's key or a customs inspector's key can come and go without ever passing the gatehouse.

Says that at about twenty-five to eleven, five bells, a gentleman in a gray homburg and a good overcoat came out of the office in a hurry and went out the main gate toward the ferry slip. Mr. Pike's light stayed on after he left.

Says Miss Ashgrove telephoned the gatehouse from the Mariners' Club at eleven o'clock, six bells, asking whether Mr. Pike was still at work, and he told her the office light was on. The club operator put her through.

Admits he never left the gatehouse after nine. At about ten past eleven, just after six bells, he saw through the window a figure in a long navy customs rain cape, hood up, walk fast under the pier lamp from the office door toward the warehouse side wicket. He took it for an inspector checking the Delacroix's seals and went back to his bottle.
Admits he took the wallet from Mr. Pike's jacket at six, before telephoning. Mr. Pike was already cold and stiff, dead for hours, and Tommy needed the eleven dollars for his rent.

deflections: *unwraps a peppermint with shaking fingers*  I tell you true, chief, it went clean out of my head. Ask me again after some coffee.
*stares out at the fog*  Eight bells, four bells, it all runs together on a night like that, Detective, sir.
Mr. Pike was good to me. That is all I got in me right now.

alibi_verification.note: His rounds story is false: the watchman's clock dial shows no station punched between 21:00 and 05:30. But the gatehouse telephone pad and Clara's admission put him at the gate telephone at 23:00, he had no reason to harm Pike, and the wallet he took came off a body already cold at 06:00. His lie covers a bottle, not a killing.

hints: Harold Pike had somewhere to be at nine this morning. Find out where, and about what: his typewriter in the front office and his tally desk in the warehouse both have something to say.
Most of the lies on this pier are not about murder. Pin every story to the clock: the police surgeon's window runs from 22:45 to 23:30.

Leonard Vance has the loudest motive and a cufflink in the archive. Show him the cufflink, then read the ferry slip tally book on the dock and the ferry clock beside it. Where was he when the window opened?
Tommy's watchman's clock says he never walked a round after nine. Show him the dial. A man who sat at the gatehouse window all night saw more than he admits.
Clara Ashgrove buried a warning about the manifests, but the gatehouse telephone pad says where she was at eleven. A motive without a window is not a case.
The weapon went back on its shelf. Look at the color smeared on its grip and ask whose gloves carry that color every working day, then check who signed out of where, and when.

Look hard at Ruth Calloway. Put together the carbon copy manifest from the warehouse tally desk, the iron ledger press from the archive shelf, the Customs House night book from the office counter, and Tommy's sighting of the caped figure.

endings.correct: Ruth Calloway takes the cuffs the way she took everything else, precisely, without a wasted word. The Harbor Commission gets Harold Pike's carbon at nine after all, and by noon six Ashgrove sailings are coming apart in the evening papers. Out on Pier Seventeen the fog lifts for the first time in three days, and nobody feels any cleaner for it.
endings.wrong_culprit: You make the arrest and the papers make the rest. Somewhere uptown a navy rain cape dries on its hook, and next week another freighter's crates sail through a clearance signed in a neat, upright hand. Harold Pike kept a carbon of everything; you missed the one that mattered.
endings.weak_proof: You had the right name and a thin file. The waterfront is full of good lawyers, and one of them walks Ruth Calloway out of the station before the coffee is cold. Motive, means, a broken alibi and a witness who saw her on the pier: the case needed all of it, and you came up short.
